# Summary {#part-practice-summary .unnumbered}

Practice begins with the user promise that a system has to keep. A workload
contract states the tasks and population in scope, the accepted outcome, the
hard constraints, and the limits on quality, latency, availability, cost, and
risk. The candidate is then a versioned served system: weights or a hosted model
revision together with its prompt, tools, retrieval, policies, runtime, routes,
and settings. Whether the workload needs a cloud service, an on-device path, a
change to the weights, or a combination is a consequence of that contract. Each
option must be evaluated against the same workload rather than justified by a
leaderboard, parameter count, or lower unit price.

The chosen option reaches production as a complete release unit. A versioned
serving contract binds runtime and compute to request semantics. A versioned
device deployment adds export, quantization, supported hardware, operating
state, and delivery. An adaptation release connects a behavior claim to governed
data, a reproducible run, evaluation, and a reversible artifact. A team that
trains its own models runs a stack of such releases, whose seams pass a data
manifest, checkpoints, trajectories, and a gated artifact. An agent
release puts a trusted controller around model proposals, tools, durable state,
authority, and effects, and it runs untrusted execution inside a sandbox
specified from a threat model. A retrieval release publishes a corpus and an
authorized query path with lineage, freshness, deletion, and citation evidence.
An evaluation release fixes the system fingerprint, the revisions of every
component that can change behavior, together with the decision claim,
population, critical slices, release gate, and rollback target before any result
is seen. None of these units is complete merely because its central component
runs.

Composition extends that fingerprint to every behavior-changing surface and
gives every released artifact an immutable identity. Each connection then needs
a boundary contract for meaning, authorization, data class, deadline, retry
ownership, idempotency, cancellation, backpressure, evidence, and recovery.
Deployment is a controlled state transition from a known baseline to a
candidate. The team proves coexistence, runs the candidate in shadow when that
can be done safely, limits it to a bounded canary, and widens exposure only when
evidence supports the next decision. Desired state, observed state, assignment,
and migration state remain distinct. Recovery follows the state that changed:
traffic rollback to the complete earlier release when it can still read current
state, restore or compensation when data or external effects changed, and a
roll-forward repair when a migration has made rollback unsafe.

Once the release is live, reliability is defined over user-visible outcomes, for
which byte-for-byte repetition and an HTTP success code are weak proxies.
Directly observed events can support an SLI and SLO for availability, latency,
policy, freshness, or effect correctness. Semantic quality usually needs a
separate probability sample, versioned rubric, calibrated judge or human review,
label deadline, and coverage report. Whether it can carry an SLO is contested;
the chapters allow one for a bounded task with representative sampling, stable
judgment, and known label delay, and treat open-ended helpfulness as diagnostic
evidence.

Where a person reviews a proposed action, the review screen acts as a control
only when approval is bound to the exact effect and revalidated at commit, and
when the system can verify the effect that followed. Product events from this
loop, such as accepts, edits, and approvals, are biased observations of a
deployed system, and one becomes a label only through a task-specific outcome or
a qualified judgment. Collection needs a declared purpose, minimum necessary
content, use authority, sampling record, partition, and deletion lineage before
it can become a versioned data product.

Operation also has to account for cost, shared capacity, and failure. Cost per
accepted task includes original attempts, retries, fallbacks, retrieval, tools,
judging, and review. A billing report arrives too late to stop a running loop,
so the runtime estimates, reserves, and admits spend before execution, then
meters and reconciles it. A qualified fallback still has to satisfy the task's
security, quality, latency, and tenancy requirements. Tenant isolation is
enforced separately across capacity, caches, indexes, credentials, tools,
egress, evidence, review, and billing. Unknown identity, policy, effect, usage,
or commit state is a named state with a declared response, such as denial,
quarantine, or escalation, and it is never counted as success. Incidents have
named roles, separate clocks, containment authority, preserved evidence,
recovery criteria, and corrective actions that are verified or recorded as
accepted risk.

An operating contract gathers those decisions into one versioned, enforceable
artifact. It connects each promise to its measurement, each budget to its
admission control, each authority to an enforcement point, each tenant boundary
to a negative test, and each incident decision to evidence. Its release record
identifies the active system, scope, owners, objectives, exceptions, validation,
rollout, rollback, residual risks, and next review. The contract makes claims
about reliability, cost, safety, and fairness specific enough to test, and it
leaves a record when a decision proves wrong; it guarantees none of those
properties. Infrastructure is dependable in this sense when its promises remain
visible, bounded, testable, and owned after the system changes and after it
fails.
